fields.h1: What Is the Fruit of the Spirit?
fields.meta_title: What Is the Fruit of the Spirit?
fields.description: Love, joy, peace, patience... The fruit of the Spirit is the character of Christ grown in the believer. Here is what each part means, where it comes from, and how it grows.
fields.body_html:
When the Bible describes what the Christian life should look like from the inside, it does not hand us a list of rules to grit our teeth and keep. It describes a harvest. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). This single verse paints the portrait of a mature Christian character — and, remarkably, it tells us where such character comes from. It is fruit, and it is the fruit of the Spirit. Understanding those two words changes everything about how we pursue the Christian life. Here is what the fruit of the Spirit is, and how it grows.

It is the character of Christ

Look closely at the nine qualities Paul lists, and you will notice they are simply a description of Jesus. He is love; he is our joy and our peace; he was patient with sinners, kind to the outcast, good, faithful to the Father, gentle with the bruised, perfectly self-controlled. The fruit of the Spirit, then, is nothing less than the character of Christ being reproduced in his people. This is God’s great purpose for every believer: that we be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). When the Spirit bears his fruit in us, he is making us like Jesus — not outwardly religious, but inwardly transformed, so that the beauty of Christ begins to show in ordinary life: in how we treat people, how we bear trouble, how we react when wronged. Paul calls it a single “fruit,” not nine “fruits,” because it is one ripening character with many facets, all growing together, all the likeness of Christ.

It is fruit, not achievement

The most important word in the phrase is “fruit.” Fruit is not manufactured; it is grown. A branch does not strain and struggle to produce apples; it simply stays joined to the tree, and the life of the tree bears fruit through it. This is exactly the picture Jesus gave: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). This is wonderfully freeing, and also humbling. It means Christian character is not finally the product of our willpower — we cannot squeeze love or peace or patience out of ourselves by effort. But it also means the way to grow is not less effort but a different kind: the effort to abide, to stay close to Christ and open to his Spirit, so that his life flows through us and bears its fruit. Hudson Taylor traced this out beautifully in Union and Communion: the fruitful life is the life joined to Christ, drawing everything from him.

It grows by the Spirit, against the flesh

Paul sets the fruit of the Spirit in sharp contrast to “the works of the flesh” — the ugly harvest our fallen nature produces on its own: “sexual immorality… enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger… envy” and the rest (Galatians 5:19–21). Every Christian feels the pull of both. The flesh still wants what it wants; the Spirit is at work to grow something better. Paul’s counsel is not “try harder to be nice” but “walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). The fruit grows as we live under the Spirit’s influence day by day — yielding to him, obeying his promptings, drawing on his power. R. A. Torrey, in The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit, stressed that holiness of character is precisely the Spirit’s work in the believer, not the believer’s achievement apart from him; the Spirit produces his own fruit in those who walk with him. Our part is to keep in step with him: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25).

A closer look at the harvest

It is worth walking slowly through the harvest Paul names, for each facet is a ray of Christ’s own character. Love stands first because it is the root of all the rest — not a feeling but a settled seeking of others’ good, the love God has “poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Joy is a gladness that does not depend on circumstances, welling up from God himself, so that we may be “sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Peace is the settled calm of a heart at rest in God, guarding us even in trouble (Philippians 4:7). Patience is the long-suffering that bears with difficult people and delays without irritation, as God has been patient with us. Kindness and goodness are love turned outward in practical care and moral integrity. Faithfulness is dependability — keeping our word, standing firm, being trustworthy as God is trustworthy. Gentleness is strength under control, the meekness of Christ who was “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). And self-control is the mastery of our own impulses, the Spirit bringing the unruly appetites under the reign of God. Set them all together and you have a portrait no human being can paint by effort — only the Spirit can grow it, and he grows it in ordinary people over ordinary years.

This gives us a searching and hopeful way to examine our own lives. We are prone to measure our spiritual health by feelings, or knowledge, or activity; but Jesus said, “you will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16). The real question is not how much we know or how busy we are for God, but whether this fruit is quietly growing — whether we are becoming, however slowly, more loving, more patient, more gentle than we used to be. And where we see the fruit still small and unripe, the answer is not despair but a fresh return to the Vine, for the same Spirit who began the work is faithful to continue it.

How the fruit ripens in us

If the fruit is grown and not manufactured, how do we cooperate with its growing? First, by staying close to Christ — abiding in him through prayer, his word, and obedience, as a branch stays in the vine. Second, by yielding daily to the Spirit, surrendering the areas of our lives we would rather keep for the flesh; Andrew Murray, in Holy in Christ, taught that our holiness is found not in ourselves but in Christ, received as we give ourselves wholly to him. Third, by walking through trials with faith, for God uses hardship to ripen this fruit — it is in difficulty that patience and gentleness and self-control are actually grown, just as fruit needs weather as well as sun. “Suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character” (Romans 5:3–4). We do not grow the fruit by staring at ourselves and measuring our progress, but by keeping our eyes on Christ and staying joined to him; the fruit follows, often more visible to others than to ourselves.

A harvest worth having

Notice, finally, what Paul says after the list: “against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:23). No one ever passed a law against too much love, too much patience, too much gentleness. This is the life every human heart, deep down, longs to have and to be around — and it is exactly what the Spirit is at work to produce in the people of God. The fruit of the Spirit is the proof that God is real and at work in a life, for no one can fake it for long; and it is the truest evidence of spiritual maturity — far truer than knowledge or giftedness or busy activity. A believer may know much and do much and still be barren; but where love and joy and peace and patience are quietly ripening, there the Spirit is surely at work.

So if you long to be more like Jesus — more loving, more patient, more at peace — do not begin by straining to produce these things from your own resources; you will only wear yourself out. Begin instead by drawing near to the One who grows them. Stay close to Christ; walk with the Spirit; yield to him the ground your flesh still claims; and trust him to bear his fruit in you in his own time. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The harvest is his to grow; our part is to abide — and the fruit of a life joined to Christ is the most beautiful thing this world ever sees. Do not be discouraged if the fruit seems slow; fruit always is. The God who is patient enough to grow an oak from an acorn is patient with you, and he has never yet abandoned a branch that stayed joined to the Vine. Abide in him, and in his own good season the harvest will surely come.
